data.title: SpaceX Stock Is a Launch Into the Abyss, Says Top Investor
data.description:
August has been good so far for SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) investors. The shares have gained 29% month-to-date, climbing back above their $135 IPO price after falling below $105. The recovery has reversed much of the post-IPO drop, with investors encouraged by the absence of heavy insider selling after 911.5 million shares first became eligible for sale on August 6.

Claim 55% Off TipRanks

Two ETFs for long or short leverage on SPCX

That milestone eased fears that a sudden increase in available shares would overwhelm demand. Sentiment received another lift last week after Elon Musk outlined plans for SpaceX to build 10 gigawatts of AI computing capacity by 2027, while Starlink reached 22 million mobile subscribers through satellite-to-cell partnerships. Another launch of 24 Starlink satellites provided an additional reminder of the company’s activity.

The rebound could face another test soon, however. On August 20, as much as 7% of the shares covered by the lockup agreement could become available for sale, with further releases scheduled in the months ahead.

As seen following the first lockup expiration, that doesn’t necessarily mean a selloff will ensue, but whether that happens or not, top investor The Value Portfolio (TVP), who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, takes a strongly bearish stance on SpaceX.

TVP argues that its first earnings report reinforced rather than weakened the concerns around the company. Although revenue rose 92% year over year, TVP says the growth does little to justify the company’s enormous valuation because it comes alongside extraordinary capital requirements. SpaceX generated about $12.5 billion in revenue during the first half of the year but spent more than $28 billion on CapEx, with AI alone absorbing over $23 billion. The investor points out that the company remains loss-making and faces a long road toward generating returns capable of supporting its valuation.

TVP sees problems across all three major businesses. The space division remains dependent on Starlink for much of its launch demand while continuing to require substantial investment. Starlink is the strongest part of the business, with subscriptions doubling year over year, but average revenue per user has fallen sharply, while Amazon’s Project Leo and other competitors threaten its market position. TVP is even more skeptical of SpaceX’s AI ambitions, believing that the company is essentially becoming a cloud provider without the proprietary silicon or customer base of larger rivals such as Google, Amazon, and Microsoft. Meanwhile, the massive spending required to build AI capacity could weigh heavily on future returns.

Based on an updated valuation model, TVP has cut the estimated value of SpaceX’s AI business from $160 billion to $80 billion, leaving the company worth roughly $260 billion – less than 15% of its $1.85 trillion current market cap.

While the investor acknowledges that SpaceX could outperform expectations, they believe its expanding share float, intensifying competition, persistent losses, and enormous CapEx burden make the current valuation difficult to defend.

TVP therefore continues to recommend against investing in SpaceX, rating the stock a Strong Sell. (To watch The Value Portfolio’s track record, click here)

That, however, gets only minimal support on Wall Street. While 2 analysts are also bears, with an additional 24 Buys and 6 Holds, the consensus view is that this stock is a Moderate Buy. The average target clocks in at $228.59, suggesting the stock will gain 63% in the months ahead. (See SPCX stock forecast)

data.title: Nvidia Stock’s Next Big Test Is Coming – Here’s What UBS Thinks
data.description:
With most of the major tech giants having already delivered their latest quarterly results, attention is now turning to the remaining big hitters. None carries more market significance than Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), which has once again reclaimed its position as the world’s most valuable company.

Claim 55% Off TipRanks

Ahead of the chipmaker’s fiscal second-quarter (July quarter) results on August 26, UBS’s Timothy Arcuri, an analyst ranked in 2nd spot among the thousands of Street stock pros, is taking an optimistic view of what lies ahead.

Arcuri expects Nvidia to comfortably beat revenue expectations, by roughly $3 billion to $4 billion, potentially putting sales as high as $94 billion-$95 billion. For FQ3, he anticipates guidance of around $107 billion-$108 billion, with actual revenue potentially topping $110 billion. The analyst sees Blackwell demand remaining steady while Rubin systems begin contributing ahead of a much bigger revenue acceleration in FQ4. That should coincide with Rubin deployments ramping toward roughly 500,000 GPUs per month as Blackwell begins to wind down.

For Arcuri, the upcoming results matter more than the broader debate surrounding AI infrastructure spending, returns on investment, and credit risks, much of which lies outside Nvidia’s direct control. He believes a strong report could give investors greater confidence that earnings can reach more than $15 per share in calendar 2027 and $20 in calendar 2028, numbers that should “keep the stock grinding higher.”

The analyst also sees Nvidia benefiting from a widening gap between demand for computing power and the industry’s ability to supply it. Although hyperscalers are sharply increasing capital spending, much of this year’s increase is being driven by higher memory prices. As a result, underlying compute supply is growing even more slowly relative to demand. That dynamic could prove to be “ultimately bullish” for Nvidia, and Arcuri believes the company could reveal another meaningful increase in its backlog when it reports.

Buybacks are another area attracting investor attention. Nvidia could potentially increase its share repurchases in calendar 2027, when Arcuri estimates the company could generate around $1 billion in free cash flow every day. However, he does not expect much new information on this front during the upcoming earnings call, given Nvidia’s recent commitment to return 50% of its free cash flow this year.

Meanwhile, Arcuri has raised his revenue forecasts from approximately $416 billion to $418 billion for calendar 2026 and from around $649 billion to $681 billion for calendar 2027. The estimates imply Data Center revenue of roughly $391 billion and $652 billion, respectively. His latest GPU unit forecasts have also increased, with 2026 shipments now expected to reach about 8.8 million, up from 8.6 million previously, and 2027 shipments projected at roughly 10.8 million, compared with 9.2 million before. These figures include CPX chips but exclude CPUs and LPUs.

Bottom line, Arcuri maintained a Buy rating on the shares along with a $280 price target, suggesting investors will be pocketing returns of 24% a year from now. (To watch Arcuri’s track record, click here)

The Street’s average target is actually higher, at $309.94, the figure makes room for 12-month returns of 38%. On the rating front, based on 36 Buys vs. 1 lone Hold, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. (See Nvidia stock forecast)

data.description:

AMD raised $4.75 billion through four bond tranches, with strong institutional demand allowing the company to price its longest-dated debt more favorably than initially expected. The funds give AMD additional financial flexibility to invest in its rapidly expanding AI hardware business and capital spending.

Meanwhile, Bank of America raised its 2030 server-CPU market forecast to more than $210 billion and named AMD a top pick. The bank argued that the growth of agentic AI will help make CPUs more important as the control layer in data centers, potentially shifting infrastructure away from a GPU-dominated model toward a more balanced CPU-GPU mix.

The gains added further sheen to a stock that is now up by 140% year-to-date, although its valuation looks quite demanding. AMD trades at roughly 31x 15-month forward earnings, compared with a 24x sector median.

However, while top investor The J Thesis (JT) concedesthat the stock is no longer a cheap way to gain exposure to AI, JT keeps a bullish stance on AMD.

It’s true the valuation has moved higher alongside the share price, but JT believes the premium remains reasonable given the company’s growth prospects, strong execution, and position in the AI ecosystem. For JT, the key question is not whether AMD is expensive in absolute terms, but whether its earnings growth can justify the valuation. At this stage, JT believes it can.

AMD’s recent performance provides much of the support for that view. Data center demand remains particularly strong, with revenue from the segment more than doubling year over year to $6.7 billion in the latest quarter. The business accounted for the majority of AMD’s total revenue, highlighting the company’s growing role in AI infrastructure. JT also points to AMD’s ability to combine rapid growth with strong profitability. Revenue increased 50% YoY, while its non-GAAP gross margin reached 56%, suggesting robust demand and meaningful pricing power.

The company is also strengthening its position for the next phase of AI growth. Its acquisition of Taalas is aimed at improving compute efficiency and AI inference capabilities, while partnerships with major technology companies such as Anthropic and Microsoft reinforce AMD’s role in the expanding AI ecosystem. JT sees these relationships as important components of AMD’s long-term competitive position and believes the company remains exposed to several attractive growth markets, including AI, data centers, and cloud computing.

JT also believes the valuation should be viewed alongside AMD’s exceptional financial performance. The company has delivered substantial revenue and earnings growth over the past year, while maintaining a solid balance sheet and healthy profitability. Although the stock commands a premium valuation, JT argues that strong earnings growth can make that premium more reasonable if the current trajectory continues. Longer term, sustained double-digit growth could allow AMD’s valuation to become less demanding as earnings catch up with the share price.

Nevertheless, there are still meaningful risks. AMD remains heavily tied to the AI investment cycle, and any deterioration in AI sentiment could pressure both the stock and its valuation. Weakness in the client and gaming business, margin compression, competition from Nvidia, and broader macroeconomic uncertainty are additional concerns.

“But that’s not my base case,” the 5-star investor summed up. “Now, my view here remains that Advanced Micro Devices successfully rides the AI-powered wave. And, quite frankly, I don’t see why it should change anytime soon. Its top and bottom-line growth remains outstanding, and this simply makes me bullish.”

Accordingly, The J Thesis rates the stock a Buy. (To watch The J Thesis’s track record, click here)

Most Street analysts agree. Based on 27 Buys vs. 6 Holds, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 26%, considering the average target clocks in at $647.04. (See AMD stock forecast)

data.title: Microsoft and Oracle: J.P. Morgan Hikes One AI Stock’s Price Target but Lowers the Other – Here’s Why
data.description:
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) have both come under considerable pressure this year as investors grapple with the enormous capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure. The spending has weighed on free cash flow at both companies, while concerns over whether these investments will ultimately deliver adequate returns have also been giving investors the jitters.

Claim 55% Off TipRanks

ORCZ: built for a short position on ORCL

Both, however, have also rebounded sharply from recent lows. Microsoft’s stronger-than-expected earnings have helped the stock turn positive on a year-to-date basis, but the results also gave a boost to Oracle, although it is still down by 22% in 2026.

Assessing the outlook for both software giants, J.P. Morgan’s Samik Chatterjee, an analyst ranked in 4th spot among the thousands of Street stock experts, takes a bullish stance on Microsoft’s growth prospects. He expects growth at both Azure and Microsoft 365 Commercial Cloud to accelerate, with the ongoing AI infrastructure build-out serving as the “key underlying driver.”

Microsoft’s cloud applications, including Copilot, essentially provide an internal source of demand for the company’s AI infrastructure. This gives Microsoft an opportunity to turn its infrastructure investments into differentiated, high-margin software offerings, while also benefiting from external demand for AI infrastructure from enterprises and AI-native companies.

Chatterjee also sees an advantage in Microsoft’s ability to offer a full-stack public cloud platform. With computing capacity constrained, the company can prioritize higher-margin opportunities instead of competing solely for “bare-metal services.” It can also direct computing resources toward its highly profitable Productivity and Business Processes segment while improving efficiency through investments in custom chips and internally developed AI models.

“We believe the portfolio mix, across infrastructure and applications, positions the company to drive high-teens revenue and earnings CAGR, but with lower support from external capital relative to hyperscaler peers,” the 5-star analyst said. “We believe the combination of high revenue and earnings growth as well as lower capital needs than peers should justify a return to the historical premium relative to the broader market, if not higher.”

As such, Chatterjee maintained an Overweight (i.e., Buy) rating on the shares, while his price target has gone from $550 to $625, implying the stock will gain 26% over the coming year. (To watch Chatterjee’s track record, click here)

Oracle presents a somewhat different proposition. Chatterjee continues to see “significant upside,” driven by a sharp acceleration in revenue as the company expands its AI infrastructure capacity, alongside the possibility of a valuation re-rating. Oracle currently trades at a substantial discount to comparable AI infrastructure and enterprise software companies, partly because investors remain concerned about the enormous capital requirements associated with its expansion.

The analyst expects Oracle’s infrastructure expansion to run ahead of the revenue generated from that capacity, leaving the company with substantial financing needs. He estimates Oracle will need to raise approximately $20 billion of capital annually on average (through FY30), including around $40 billion in FY27. Chatterjee also acknowledges that his capital expenditure forecasts are above management’s expectations because he anticipates sustained AI infrastructure demand and further investment to support growth.

That said, the analyst also takes a bullish stance here too. “Despite the increase in the debt position to fund the infrastructure build, we see sizeable upside to the equity valuation for the company led by a combination of profit growth as well as a re-rating of the valuation multiple,” Chatterjee summed up.

While the analyst rates ORCL as Overweight too, given the enormous capital intensity and financing requirements of Oracle’s AI build-out, combined with the move to a December 2027 valuation date, his price target has been lowered from $210 to $200. Nevertheless, there’s still potential upside of 33% from current levels.

Both these stocks get plenty of favorable reviews elsewhere on the Street, with both claiming Strong Buy consensus ratings. MSFT’s average price target stands at $564.49, implying shares will climb by 14% in the months ahead. ORCL stock’s is projected to gain 71.5%, given the average target clocks in at $258.14. data.title: ‘It’s Not That Simple,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) stock appears to be making a strong comeback after last month’s sharp pullback. Since hitting a low on July 29, the shares have climbed 31.5%, helped by what now looks like an overly aggressive selloff amid bullish industry forecasts, rapidly growing AI-driven demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and expectations that structural memory shortages could persist through 2027. At the same time, concerns over competition from Chinese memory makers appear to be easing.

Claim 55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

Looking at the current situation, an investor with the moniker of Khaveen Investments believes Micron can continue benefiting from the surge in AI-related memory demand. However, Khaveen also sees some risks and competitive pressure ahead that make the investment case less clear-cut.

Khaveen concedes Micron’s recent growth has been impressive, with revenue up 346% year over year in FQ3. DRAM has been the biggest contributor, while NAND has also grown strongly. Within DRAM, HBM has emerged as a major growth engine, driven by soaring demand from AI data centers. Khaveen expects demand for HBM to remain strong as major cloud providers continue the AI buildout, given the need for large amounts of high-performance memory.  

Memory prices have also continued to rise as demand has outpaced supply. Khaveen believes this dynamic should support Micron’s revenue and margins in the near term. The company is also significantly expanding its manufacturing capacity, particularly in the U.S., while its U.S. manufacturing investments are being supported by roughly $6.4 billion in direct federal funding under the CHIPS Act.

The manufacturing capacity expansion should allow the company to better meet growing demand. It should also give Micron a more geographically diversified production base and reduce its reliance on Taiwan. Even so, Khaveen expects supply to remain tight for certain products through 2029, suggesting favorable conditions in the memory market could persist for several more years.

While all the above points to a bullish outlook, Khaveen also highlights the competition Micron faces. It remains the third-largest DRAM supplier behind Samsung and SK hynix, and the investor expects its competitive position to weaken over time as China’s CXMT rapidly expands its production capacity.

Khaveen also sees some uncertainty around Micron’s product leadership. While the company appears capable of remaining competitive in next-generation HBM products, its planned GDDR7 speeds trail those of Samsung and SK hynix. Patent litigation is another potential downside risk.

Overall, then, while Khaveen remains positive on Micron’s long-term growth prospects, particularly because of AI-driven HBM demand and its major capacity expansion plans, the stock’s strong growth expectations are balanced by rising competition and the other risks mentioned above.

To this end, Khaveen rates MU stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Khaveen Investments’ track record, click here)

However, overall, the Street disagrees with that stance. While one analyst remains on the sidelines with a Hold rating, all 29 other recent reviews are also positive, making the consensus view a Strong Buy. At $1,569.07, the average target suggests shares will gain 61.5% over the coming year. (See MU stock forecast)

data.description:
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) shares have experienced extreme volatility since their June 12 IPO. After rising above $225, the stock plunged more than 50% to around $104 in August, pressured by valuation concerns, heavy spending in its first earnings report, and insider lockup expirations that added hundreds of millions of shares to the market.

  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

Yet the stock surged just as the first lockup expired, releasing 911.5 million shares for trading and effectively doubling the public float. Investors had expected the influx to weigh on the stock, but the opposite happened. It was the first of several staggered releases, with another 319 million shares set to become available on August 20, followed by additional releases in September.

The momentum continued on Monday, and while the stock has slipped into the red on Tuesday, the shares are up by 26% over the past week. Against this backdrop, top investor Tech Stock Pros (TSP), who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, wonders whether the rally is temporary or the beginning of a “longer winning streak.”

TSP sees SpaceX’s Q2 results as evidence that its core businesses remain strong, but significant concerns remain around the scale of spending required to support the company’s ambitions.

Revenue surged 92% year over year to $7.8 billion, beating expectations, while all three segments outperformed forecasts. Connectivity revenue rose 66%, AI revenue jumped 247%, and the AI business generated positive adjusted EBITDA for the first time. Space also delivered stronger-than-expected growth, with 78 launches during the first half of 2026.

However, the investor remains particularly concerned about SpaceX’s spending. Q2 capex reached $18.4 billion, including $15.8 billion for AI infrastructure, while management expects similarly elevated spending in the next two quarters. TSP is also skeptical of the company’s aggressive targets for AI compute, Starlink and Starship, arguing that many will be difficult to achieve and that, just like Tesla, SpaceX is being valued on “future promises” rather than current fundamentals.

The AI business is the biggest concern, given the enormous capital requirements and intense competition from other major players. TSP also expects heavy spending to remain a recurring issue for investors, even as SpaceX’s space and Starlink businesses continue to perform well. Those businesses provide a significant competitive advantage, with SpaceX controlling roughly 82% of U.S. space launches and more than 80% of global mass-to-orbit.

The key change, however, has been in the market’s reaction to those risks. As seen, the stock remained resilient after 911.5 million shares were released through the first major lockup expiration, when investors had expected increased supply to add further pressure to the shares. Instead, the stock rallied sharply.

For TSP, that shift in sentiment – not a fundamental improvement in the underlying story – is what changes the investment case. “We see space momentum building back up after last week’s lockup period failed to crash the stock, which is a bullish signal in our book for a company at a $1.75T valuation,” the 5-star investor summed up. “We see more room for SpaceX to run up into its next lockup expiry and advise investors to think of the stock as a swing trade for 2H.”

Accordingly, TSP has upgraded SPCX’s rating from Sell to Buy. (To watch Tech Stock Pros’ track record, click here)

data.title: ‘A Burden Lifted,’ Says Top Analyst About Nvidia Stock
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is helping put together as much as $500 billion in financing for the next wave of AI infrastructure, joining forces with major financial players including Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR.

Claim 55% Off TipRanks

NVDS: built for a short position on NVDA

The company said the initiative essentially gives AI-related hardware and computing capacity status as an investable asset class, with the financing designed to help customers such as AI labs and cloud companies obtain the GPUs, data centers, and other infrastructure they need.

The money could ultimately fund new facilities for deploying and cooling large-scale computing systems, as well as manufacturing capacity for the chips required to run them. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the initiative as a “major milestone for Nvidia and the AI industry.”

BofA’s Vivek Arya, an analyst who ranks among the top 2% on Wall Street, also likes the sound of the arrangement, viewing this development favorably. “We await further details, but our first take is a positive one – the burden sits with the consortium, not NVDA’s balance sheet,” the 5-star analyst said.

Arya believes the arrangement could also represent a meaningful change from Nvidia’s previous approach to customer financing, which has faced criticism over the potential for circular funding. Although he estimates vendor financing represents only around 15% of Nvidia’s projected $470 billion in free cash flow over 2026-27, he expects the company’s next earnings call to offer greater clarity on how much it intends to participate in such arrangements going forward. Arya believes that the chip giant’s FCF can be “better directed to a stock that trades at significantly depressed valuation.”

A key part of his positive thesis is the durability of Nvidia’s GPUs as financial assets. Arya argues that chips capable of being moved between operators should retain meaningful residual value, particularly because Nvidia’s CUDA platform can extend their practical usefulness. That could result in relatively favorable depreciation and resale economics, making the underlying hardware more attractive to investors. “NVDA guarantees asset quality, not the debt — turning the bear’s depreciation worry into the enabling feature,” the analyst went on to say.

Meanwhile, the new pool of capital could further accelerate AI infrastructure spending by addressing a constraint that has shifted from demand to funding and supply. Smaller AI developers, specialized cloud operators, and sovereign buyers could gain access to capital for GPUs, data-center capacity, and power, potentially reducing concerns around whether new infrastructure will find customers. Arya says this supports BofA’s longer-term view of a $1.7 trillion AI systems market by 2030.

The analyst nevertheless sees several issues that investors need to monitor. Funding commitments still need to translate into actual spending by customers, while moving financial risk elsewhere does not eliminate doubts over the returns generated by AI infrastructure. Electricity availability, regulation, and rising costs remain additional obstacles, and ever more complicated financing arrangements could make the underlying AI buildout harder for investors to evaluate.

Nvidia’s own involvement is another unanswered question. Arya expects the new structure to reduce the company’s need to put its own balance sheet behind customers, but if Nvidia ultimately has to contribute more cash than expected, its free cash flow could be reduced, leaving less available for share buybacks.

So, what does all of that mean for investors? Arya still considers the stock a “top pick,” maintaining a Buy rating on NVDA shares, while his $350 price objective points toward 12-month returns of 59%. (To watch Arya’s track record, click here)

The Street’s average target is not quite as high, but at $309.94, still makes room for one-year gains of 41%. On the rating front, based on a lopsided mix of 36 Buys and 1 Hold, the analyst consensus views this stock as a Strong Buy. (See Nvidia stock forecast)

Sereda also sees several potential catalysts. Micron’s HBM4 shipments for Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform are ramping, while its LPDDR5X solution for Nvidia’s GB300 could open additional data-center opportunities. Meanwhile, growing demand for data-center SSDs could support NAND revenue and margins.

Then there’s a very appealing valuation. Sereda considers Micron undervalued at roughly 5.7 times forward FY2027 earnings. He expects analysts to raise their estimates as recent positive revisions and upcoming growth catalysts become reflected in forecasts. He also believes the market is underestimating Micron’s ability to sustain earnings growth beyond FY2027, with the current valuation implying a sharper slowdown than he considers likely.

Sereda does acknowledge a key risk: if memory demand weakens unexpectedly, pricing and margins could deteriorate rapidly. In that scenario, the changing market environment could trigger a more bearish valuation of the stock.

However, that is not currently playing out, and the investment case remains robust. “I see no reasonable explanation for why the peak is already in,” the 5-star investor summed up. “In other words, the market environment and the willingness of Micron’s key customers to agree to such substantial upfront payments suggest to me that the cycle is plateauing, but it is not over yet. data.description:

There were, however, plenty of encouraging elements in the report. Rocket Lab generated a record $234 million in Q2 revenue, $3.12 million above expectations, representing a 62% year-over-year increase and surpassing the previous quarterly record by $34 million. The company also ended the period with a record backlog of $2.36 billion. Non-GAAP gross margin came in at 41.5%, comfortably ahead of the 38% analysts had anticipated.

The outlook was also stronger than expected. Management guided for Q3 revenue of $250 million to $265 million, compared with the Street’s $235.9 million forecast.

Still, the results contained several areas that appear to have disappointed investors. Rocket Lab’s net loss narrowed to $49 million from $66 million a year earlier, but the company still posted a loss of $0.08 per share, exceeding the $0.06 loss analysts had forecast.

Margins are also expected to weaken in the near term. Management expects Q3 GAAP gross margin of 29% to 31%, down considerably from 36.1% in Q2. Non-GAAP gross margin is projected at 35% to 37%, compared with the 41.5% achieved in Q2. Ongoing investment in the development of the Neutron rocket is also likely to keep Rocket Lab unprofitable in the near term.

Despite the market’s negative reaction, Cowen’s Gautam Khanna, an analyst who ranks among the top 1% on Wall Street, remains a RKLB bull. Khanna noted several takeaways from the quarter.

The most important development, according to Khanna, is that Neutron remains on schedule to reach the launchpad in Q4. However, he believes the rocket could spend another four to eight weeks at the launch complex before its first flight, potentially pushing the inaugural launch into next year.

Khanna nevertheless sees strong evidence that demand for Neutron remains intact. Rocket Lab already has a dedicated booking from Kepler and a planned Flatellite mission for the U.S. Space Force. He notes that management does not expect demand to fade despite the emergence of competing launch systems such as SpaceX’s Starship and Blue Origin’s New Glenn.

The company has also secured bookings ahead of Neutron’s first flight, while government demand for launch services continues to expand. The National Security Space Launch program, for example, recently increased the ceiling for its Phase 3 Lane 1 contracts to $17 billion from $5.6 billion.

Rocket Lab’s Q2 Launch Services revenue of $45 million fell short of the Street’s $71 million estimate, although Khanna noted that the comparison was distorted because a substantial portion of the revenue associated with two HASTE launches had already been recognized in earlier periods.

The Space Systems business provided another source of optimism. Bookings remain robust, highlighted by a $397 million Flatellite contract awarded in July and more than $160 million in contracts to build three geostationary-orbit satellites. Khanna expects revenue from these awards to be recognized over roughly four years, generally following the structure used for other government programs such as SDA Tranche 2 and Tranche 3.

There are still near-term margin pressures to contend with. Mynaric and an unfavorable change in business mix are expected to weigh on consolidated gross margin during Q3. Khanna expects the mix to become more favorable again in Q4.

Khanna also pointed out that Rocket Lab does not view the Iridium deal – the proposed acquisition remains on track to close in mid-2027 – as necessarily representing the final step in its broader ambitions for satellite constellations.

All told, Khanna maintained a Buy rating on RKLB shares, while his $120 price target suggests the stock will gain 50% in the months ahead. (To watch Khanna’s track record, click here)

data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) stock is rising in Monday’s session offering respite for investors after last week’s latest quarterly results showed that, sometimes, on Wall Street, very good is just not good enough. With the market now jittery about memory stocks after a major rally driven by favorable supply-demand dynamics, an investor using the pseudonym Simple Investment Ideas (SII) acknowledges that the industry has entered a “risky area of the memory cycle.”

However, SII remains bullish on SNDK, arguing that the market is misjudging how long Sandisk’s earnings growth can persist before the industry returns to more normalized conditions. SII also believes investors are underestimating the strength and quality of the earnings base the company has established during this period.

The thesis centers on Sandisk shifting its business away from consumer products such as flash drives and SD cards and toward enterprise SSDs, which should give the company greater exposure to AI infrastructure spending. The move away from consumer products, combined with multi-year volume commitments, pricing floors, and financial guarantees, should also reduce the company’s exposure to NAND price volatility. While these agreements do not create a subscription-like model for NAND, they should provide a stronger foundation for volumes, revenue, and free cash flow than Sandisk has historically had, potentially supporting a higher valuation multiple than would normally be justified at the peak of a memory cycle.

The broader opportunity is linked to the changing role of memory in AI. Training remains heavily concentrated around compute and high-bandwidth memory, but large-scale inference presents different requirements. AI agents repeatedly need to access context, query vector databases, and store growing quantities of generated information, creating demand for very large storage capacity located sufficiently close to processors to deliver high input/output performance.

“Thus,” says SII, “enterprise NAND will function as active inference infrastructure rather than merely as an inactive repository for archival purposes.”

As far as valuation is concerned, Sandisk trades at roughly 5.8 times forward earnings, broadly in line with Micron at 6.1 times but above Kioxia at around 4 times. These low valuations reflect investors’ expectations that memory companies are near peak earnings and that rising NAND supply from process migrations and new capacity will pressure prices and margins in 2027. The investor generally agrees that supply conditions should improve in the second half of 2027, but believes the impact will be less severe than in previous cycles. Contracted volumes, pricing floors and relatively capital-light expansion opportunities should help NAND suppliers limit the extent of margin compression.

“I am not suggesting that Sandisk needs to transition into a non-cyclical entity,” SII explained. “Rather, I am simply advocating for investors to recognize that contracted demand and improved cash conversion will result in a more resilient business model than that of traditional NAND suppliers.”

To this end, SII rates SNDK stock a Buy. (To watch SII’s track record, click here)

Pierce came away confident in the investment case. “We continue to see RIVN as a winner in the ICE to EV transition, with RIVN getting minimal credit for strong R2 demand signals and early execution as well as zero credit for their autonomy aspirations with the most common bear arguments we hear losing momentum,” the analyst said.

The more difficult challenge will be production. Rivian still needs to demonstrate that it can manufacture the R2 at sufficient scale to satisfy demand. That issue featured prominently in investor questions, although management expressed confidence in its supply base and its ability to support additional second- and third-shift production.

Pierce also sees autonomy as a potentially important source of upside during the second half of 2026. Consumer interest in autonomous driving appears to be accelerating, as demonstrated by enthusiasm among Waymo riders and increasing adoption of Tesla’s FSD (Full Self-Driving) technology. In Pierce’s view, Rivian’s autonomy opportunity remains largely overlooked.

While the test drives did not allow investors to fully assess Rivian’s current autonomy capabilities because they were restricted to city driving, Pierce sees a “rich catalyst path ahead.” These include point-to-point autonomy, the launch of a LIDAR-equipped R2 variant, and a second Autonomy and AI Investor event, all expected in the second half of the year.

Lessons from the R1 program are also influencing the newer model, including a more streamlined selection of buyer configurations that could help Rivian achieve its targeted gross-margin improvement.

Meanwhile, Rivian’s Universal Hands-Free driving system represents the “first autonomy domino to fall.” Future products are expected to incorporate internally developed silicon, potentially enabling quicker development cycles while improving the margin profile.

As for the bears’ arguments, Pierce says these are now “struggling to maintain traction.”

“Broader EV adoption concerns are a common theme, but EV adoption is set to lap its toughest comp in 3Q26 clearing the growth path. The R2 launch has been hiccup free to date, answering the execution question, and any near term balance sheet concerns are now muted as well. Investor skepticism towards autonomy is fair considering RIVN only offered an adaptive cruise control type product just one year ago, but the increasing pace of product introductions favors the bulls,” the analyst summed up.

data.title: This Is What Needs to Change for Meta Stock, Says Investor
data.description:
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) stock got punished badly following its latest earnings release, falling 8% as investors reacted to an EPS miss, a steep decline in free cash flow, $2.4 billion in legal proceedings charges, and a higher minimum capex outlook tied to its aggressive AI infrastructure investments.

But are those really the reasons why the market reacted so negatively? Investor Vinay Utham argues that the drop wasn’t ultimately connected to cash flow (Meta’s was still positive) or capex (Meta’s wasn’t raised as much as Amazon, for instance) but that the market’s real concern lay elsewhere.

According to Utham, the key issue was that Meta “failed to provide a concrete demand signal” to justify its additional AI spending. Other hyperscalers offered investors clear evidence that their massive infrastructure investments were being supported by strong customer demand.

Microsoft, for example, reported $678 billion in commercial remaining performance obligations (RPOs), an 84% year-over-year increase, with sequential growth also coming entirely from customers outside the major frontier-model firms. Amazon reported a $496 billion AWS backlog, representing a $132 billion sequential increase, while Alphabet highlighted a $514 billion cloud backlog alongside a significant acceleration in cloud revenue. Alphabet stock got hit too, but Utham thinks the negative market reaction appeared to be a result of its open-ended 2027 capex outlook and negative quarterly free cash flow rather than weak demand.

Meta, by contrast, reported just $1.16 billion in deferred revenue and slower year-over-year growth in both average revenue per person (ARPP) and daily active people (DAP) across its family of apps – two metrics management had previously linked to its AI investments. Growth also slowed in ad impressions and total advertising revenue, further weakening the evidence that its AI spending was translating into stronger demand or monetization.

In previous quarters, Utham thought Meta’s AI investments were being validated by improving results, leading him to argue that the stock was suffering from “post-metaverse stress disorder.” This quarter, however, the concerns appeared more justified. While Meta’s peers demonstrated clear reasons to continue ramping up AI spending, Meta failed to offer a comparable demand signal, creating a “double whammy” that helps explain the market’s unusually harsh reaction.

Meanwhile, potential new revenue streams, such as renting excess computing capacity and its coding agent, could help, but they are either unproven or too early to assess.

Oracle has been among the most aggressive companies in pursuing AI-related infrastructure investment. Oracle’s capital expenditures exceeded 170% of operating cash flow in the latest quarter, the highest ratio among its peers. Its high leverage and aggressive expansion have also contributed to one of the sector’s highest stock betas, leaving shareholders particularly vulnerable to a broader cloud-sector or stock market downturn.

As such, although the share price drop might attract investors seeking a bargain, Dimitrov cautions that it is not necessarily undervalued. “The drop in Oracle’s stock over the past year does not mean that investors are buying it at a discount,” he summed up. “In absolute terms it is trading at much lower levels and far lower multiples, but there are solid reasons for this and investors are now taking much greater risks. The record high CDS spread, the uncertainty regarding future returns of cloud infrastructure investments and potential moral hazard risks will all continue to overshadow ORCL’s future share price returns.”

To this end, Dimitrov rates the stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Dimitrov’s track record, click here)

Most on the Street, however, disagree with that stance. Based on a mix of 27 Buys and 4 Holds, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. There are plenty of gains projected here. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 76%, considering the average target clocks in at $258.50. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Don’t Get Left Behind,’ Says Top Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk’s (NASDAQ:SNDK) massive rally came unstuck last month, as chip stocks experienced a sharp reversal in fortune. A combination of fears over AI spending, concerns over eventual loss of pricing power in the cyclical memory industry, profit-taking and a revenue guide that slightly missed Wall Street’s lofty expectations have all contributed to the pullback. As such, the stock now sits 48% below the all-time high reached in June.

Claim 55% Off TipRanks

Two ETFs for long or short leverage on SNDK

Of course, investors now must choose whether the stock is destined to sink lower or whether the depressed price action presents a lopsided opportunity.

Looking at the NAND Flash specialist’s prospects, top investor JR Research thinks the latter is the case.

JR, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, believes Sandisk is gradually positioning itself as an AI infrastructure play rather than simply a traditional storage company. While its new high-bandwidth flash (HBF) technology is not a direct replacement for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), it could complement HBM as AI workloads become increasingly demanding, creating a potentially significant new growth opportunity.

The investor sees AI inference as a particularly important catalyst. As AI agents become more sophisticated and models grow larger, demand for memory and storage is likely to increase, potentially expanding the addressable market for HBF. JR believes Sandisk’s opportunity could be supported by a potential $500 billion TAM through 2027, meaning near-term revenue growth may remain robust rather than immediately becoming a concern.

Importantly, the market appears to already be pricing in a substantial slowdown. Revenue growth is expected to fall sharply from fiscal 2028, despite potentially triple-digit growth through the next fiscal year. JR views that disconnect as an opportunity, particularly if HBF emerges as Sandisk’s next major growth driver. Sandisk’s investor day on August 13 should provide greater visibility on that front.

The investor also points to Sandisk’s valuation as evidence that considerable pessimism is already reflected in the stock. At around six times forward earnings, the market appears to be anticipating weaker pricing power and earnings normalization well ahead of time.

At the same time, Sandisk has strengthened its position through long-term NBM (new business model) agreements, with weighted-average terms of four to five years, floor pricing and financial guarantees providing greater revenue visibility. These agreements should help reduce the company’s historical exposure to cyclical volatility.

While pricing leverage could weaken from 2028 as hyperscaler capital spending normalizes, JR believes SNDK’s valuation has “really captured the recent pessimism.”

“I believe the bottoming opportunity in the memory and storage stocks is now becoming timely for investors who are looking to get on board before they pick up pace again,” the 5-star investor summed up.

With this in mind, JR has now upgraded his SNDK rating from Hold (i.e., Neutral) to Buy. (To watch JR’s track record, click here)

That is also the most common take on Wall Street right now. The stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on a mix of 13 Buys and 3 Holds. At $2,220, the average price target offers 12-month upside of 83%. (See SNDK stock forecast)
